learning_outcomes.text: Learning the basic notions of differential and integral calculus.
Learn the theory and tools of mathematical analysis of real functions of a real variable. In particular, the concept of limit and convergence, differential and integral calculus.

Be able to solve classic problems such as, for example, drawing the qualitative graph of a function, solving maximum/minimum problems in one variable, knowing how to calculate areas using integrals, solving some ordinary differential equations.
Be able to make a mathematical deduction and write it in the form of a proof.
Be able to appropriately use the language and terminology of the subject. Be able to independently develop and express deductive reasoning in a mathematical context.

Learn how to approach the study of a scientific, and particularly mathematical, subject, recognizing one's doubts and seeking an explanation, both independently and with the help of teachers and other students.

The student will learn several important mathematical concepts and will develop the calculation and manipulation skills of the most common objects of Mathematical Analysis: among these, limits, derivatives, integrals, and series.

Through examples related to applied sciences, the student will be able to appreciate the importance of Mathematical Analysis in the scientific field and not just as a discipline in itself, thus broadening their cultural horizons.

The student will be able to approach with sufficient rigor various but significant demonstrative methods of Mathematical Analysis to refine logical skills. Many examples of proofs with intuitive explanations will be provided to engage students and stimulate them to achieve the goal independently.

By studying Mathematical Analysis and testing themselves through guided exercises and learning tests, the student will gradually learn to communicate with rigor and clarity. They will learn that using correct language is one of the most important means for effective communication, not only in the mathematical field.
Students, especially the most eager, will be encouraged to delve deeper into certain topics.

syllabus_topics: Logic and set theory: propositional logic, set theory, functions, order relations
Number sets: the field of real numbers, natural numbers, relative integers, rational numbers, completeness axiom and consequences, summations, complex numbers
Real functions: extremes of functions, monotonic functions, function transformations and symmetries, elementary functions

Limits of real functions of a real variable: the extended number line, general definition of limit (with neighborhoods), limits of numerical sequences, operations on limits and main theorems on limits, limits of monotonic functions and sequences

Continuous functions: definition, operations on continuous functions and main theorems on continuous functions, topological properties for sequences, bisection method and theorems of zeros, intermediate values and Weierstrass
Numerical series: series with positive terms and convergence criteria, series of any sign
Derivative: derivation rules and derivatives of elementary functions

Applications of differential calculus: Fermat's rule, Lagrange's Theorem, monotonicity criteria for differentiable functions, convex functions and characterization using the first and second derivatives, Taylor's formula
Riemann integral: definition and main properties, fundamental theorem of integral calculus, methods for calculating definite integrals, indefinite integrals and indefinite integration methods
assessment_rules: The written exam is evaluated based on the logic followed by the student, the correctness of the procedure, the adequacy of the proposed solution, and the use of appropriate language. An oral exam is at the discretion of the lecturer and is not always mandatory. If an oral exam is given, it will evaluate the student's ability to elaborate an adequate response, promptness in answering questions correctly, and ability to infer new knowledge from acquired notions.
